utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before I ask the usher to escort the witness into the courtroom, I'd like to address both parties before the cross-examination starts. The Chamber expresses its concern on the course the presentation of evidence took this week. The Chamber notes that mainly in relation to, I would say, the last witness, that a case is not decided on the basis of impressions, without a clear and proper factual foundation; that the presentation of opinion and analysis of a witness mainly informs the Chamber about the fact that that witness has formed such an opinion or has developed such analysis. What the Chamber needs are facts to form its own opinion and to develop its own analysis. The parties may have understood this well on the basis of an analysis of the questions the Chamber has put to the Witness Bjelobrk. That's my first observation. Second one: The Chamber has carefully listened to the observations made by Mr. Krajisnik, who offered verification of the answers of the witness -- the witness has given by producing the stenographic notes of meetings or sessions. The Chamber invites the Defence to provide all those portions of the stenographic notes that could serve to correct or perhaps even contradict any of the answers, whether in statement or in testimony, given by the witness. They can be submitted with a clear reference to the relevant part of the testimony or the statement. Here again, the Defence should also be aware that the Chamber focuses on facts rather than on anything else. Once the relevant portions of the minutes have been translated, the Chamber will first of all invite the parties to agree on whether they accept the stenographic notes to be a reliable source of information, and ask their views on the probative value of those portions. Then the Chamber will decide whether or not it will admit those portions in evidence and whether Mr. Bjelobrk should be recalled to be examined on those stenographic notes. My next observation is about the cross-examination this afternoon. Mr. Stewart, the Chamber would like to guide you to deal with any subject in order of relevance, most relevance, the most relevant issues first. The cross-examination should be as brief as reasonably possible. In view of the specific knowledge Mr. Krajisnik may have, as the Chamber understood from his yesterday's observations, the Chamber would, exceptionally, allow Mr. Krajisnik to put questions to the witness which he feels, and of course, perhaps, after having consulted counsel, he would be better fit to put to this witness. At the end of today's hearing, the Chamber will consider whether the witness will have to be recalled for any further cross-examination, and the Chamber may decide to hear the Defence on the subjects still to be dealt with in such further cross-examination before making its determination. These are the matters I would like to bring to the attention of the parties before I ask Mr. Usher, as I do now, to escort Mr. Bjelobrk into the courtroom. Mr. Hannis, could you meanwhile inform the Chamber on whether the minutes of the 8th Session, as we find them in the Treanor material, is a complete copy or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is not. It contains certain highlighted portions of those minutes. So I would ask that we get a different number for the -- pardon me, the version that was presented to Mr. Bjelobrk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you give a number to the exhibit containing the minutes of the 8th Session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The exhibit number will be P406.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Bjelobrk, may I first of all remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Then you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Stewart, who is Defence counsel. Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, when you -- good afternoon. When you gave evidence yesterday, or in fact I think it was the day before, this particular point, you referred to the SDS having created what you've called a system of protection. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that. Good afternoon to you, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you said -- and this is, for the reference, at page 85 of Tuesday's transcript. You said: In your opinion, this was an idea developed by the leadership, first of all, because the common citizens on the ground did not have any special purposes for protection; and secondly, as you will see from one of the transcripts here, is what you said, that the drawing of the map in this sense was being done by a very narrow circle of the people from among the leadership of the SDS. Mr. Bjelobrk, first of all, when you were referring to the drawing of the map in this sense, which was your phrase, did you have in mind a specific map or were you talking in a rather more general or almost figurative sense about the drawing of the map?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm recalling the transcript that was shown to me before these court hearings, and you heard that yesterday as well, that there were not only two, but three persons talking about the drawing of maps. So it wasn't only Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness's other microphone please be turned on, because we cannot hear him properly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you could also adjust the microphone, Mr. Usher. They're both on, but perhaps they could a bit closer to the witness. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So the position is that your -- such knowledge as you have about the drawing of the map, in that sense, is derived from what you have heard from that intercept?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I knew in principle, generally speaking, from the spring and summer of 1991, stems from the numerous conversations I had with SDS MPs. I did not have material evidence of these talks, but then I heard these transcripts when preparing for this session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What I'm trying to get clear, Mr. Bjelobrk, is that back at the time of the events in question, so during 1991 and 1992, you were never present when any such map was discussed or being considered by SDS leadership, were you?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not present then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And when you say that the drawing of the map in this sense was being done by a very narrow circle of the people from among the leadership of the SDS, is it also correct that you have no personal knowledge of who among the leadership of the SDS was engaged in such an exercise beyond what you gather from the intercepts?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I inferred what I did primarily on the basis of the summer of 1991, but I do agree with you that it is not based on any direct Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond participation of mine in any such thing, or do I have any material evidence. However, I had series of talks with SDS MPs, and also a lot of other information. And to be quite frank, it was only logical in terms of everything what was happening in the area, in the field; and, on the other hand, these new establishments were being formed and this led me to infer what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But no -- none of these MPs came and told you, for example, that they were -- had been directly involved in consideration of any specific map, did they?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can now speak from memory only. I did not hear such positions explicitly, but I could conclude on the basis of the conversations I had that regionalisation, as it was called then, was being considered and that in the initial stage it involved the drawing of maps too. I don't know who was doing it, and I did not know where they were doing it, but I did know that it was a privilege of a narrow circle of persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And in your evidence on Tuesday, and this is at page 86 of the transcript, you were asked specifically about paragraph 20 of your own statement, about the process of regional organisation and protection. And you said, among other things, you said: They - that's the SDS - were formulating their responses to the initiatives of others, and they merely had the need to respond to that in defence. Now, when you refer to the initiatives of others there, can you specify what "others" you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SDS had a partner, or rather, a potential challenge in terms of formulating such a response, and that was the SDA and the HDZ. I shall try to explain to you now what I meant by "defence." It was an organised political mechanism, and it seems that one only responds to what others are doing. But actually, it is one's own positions that are being worked out. That was the dominant tactic of the SDS, confirmed by its top people, including Mr. Krajisnik, in his January 1992 interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You said, then, same answer, at page 86 of Tuesday's transcript, you said that in 1991 there was a thesis, according to which each ethnicity will or would have its own government and run its own government, which means that you will have government mechanisms in individual areas and you will separate the ethnicities along those lines. That thesis was not exclusive to the members of the SDS, was it?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did point out - and I would like to ask you if we could possibly check this - both in my statement and also in the answer I gave into this microphone, that this was the thesis of the SDS only.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So you say there was nobody else in Bosnia and Herzegovina, apart from members of the SDS, who contemplated at any point each ethnicity having its own government and running its own government?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll give you a precise answer. Both of the other two national parties were involved in a similar thing, and that became obvious when, in the HDZ, the leadership was changed. It was Mr. Kljuic specifically. I think that this is around the new year, that is to say, the end of 1991/1992. In the SDA, this appeared at the beginning of the war, and then it culminated, as far as I can remember, in the spring of 1993, when a working paper on the Islamic Republic came out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You talked quite a lot in your evidence about the - and I'm summarising - the difficulties of operation of the Bosnia and Herzegovina Assembly and what you described as various bits of obstructive behaviour. You said, and this is page 88 and 89 of the transcript on Tuesday, when you were talking about what you described as obstruction by Mr. Krajisnik. And you said: "Finally, when there was some hope of the Assembly being able to vote for the proposal, the SDS representative said that only those items can be placed on the agenda where consensus would be achieved by all the three ethnicities, and the second proposal was that 51 per cent of the vote was not going to be enough for a proposal to be adopted because one ethnicity was, in their words, too loud. In the end, all this meant that the work of the Assembly had to be obstructed." Now, would you agree, Mr. Bjelobrk, that the period that you were describing, these were, to understate it, these were very tense times, with deep underlying differences among the different nationalities represented in the Bosnia and Herzegovina Assembly? That was basic to the situation, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, as far as I can see here in the transcript, I'm afraid that this is not an accurate quotation of what I said, that is to say, page 88 and 89, so I'll try to clarify it once again. There are two situations that existed. One --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can I just stoup for a moment, Mr. Bjelobrk. When you say it's not an accurate translation of what you said, are you managing to refer back to pages 88 and 89 of Tuesday's transcript?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: With pleasure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No. Are you? Were you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, I take it that Mr. Stewart is quoting from the exact wording as has been transcribed from this meeting. If you say that it is certainly not correct, then this Chamber -- please indicate so this Chamber has an opportunity to have the tapes checked. But please answer the question. And if you really insist that this is not what you said, please let us know so we can check it. Now you may continue your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm very much obliged, Your Honour. May I just say, in the second line of what Your Honour has just said, I take it Mr. Stewart is quoting from the exact wording as has been transcribed from this meeting. I think Your Honour means hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's a meeting, of course, in a sense, but here we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bjelobrk. I am doing my best simply to read 100 per cent accurately as I can manage from the transcript, so please take it that, unless anybody suggests otherwise, that is the position. So that was what you were saying, and my question, just to remind you, was that: This was a period of deep underlying differences among the different nationalities represented in the Bosnia and Herzegovina Assembly, and that was basic to the situation at the time, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll give you a precise answer to your question. I thank you, Mr. President, for your intervention. So the summer Assembly was basically characterised by the fact that members of the SDS walked out before the debate started. After that, when the autumn assemblies were being prepared, the collegium defined the agenda in the following terms: That only where consensus is reached by all three national parties can a certain item be placed on the agenda. The principle of legality in both cases was 51 per cent. That was the required majority according to the rules of procedure. At any rate, the SDS MPs and the leadership of the SDS explained that this did not -- this decision could not be legitimate because even if it did have a 51 per cent majority it could not be legitimate if one people was totally opposed to it. Another question you put to me. There's no doubt that there were increased tensions in the summer of 1991 in Bosnia and Herzegovina, primarily because people did not like at all the fact that the presidents of the Yugoslav republics had failed in their negotiations concerning the future of Yugoslavia, and there was a great deal of discussion about this in the media and in the public in general. These tensions were also contributed to by the unproductive work of the Assembly. So the questions that were raised were very difficult to resolve. On the other hand, in my opinion, if you look at another important characteristic of the general situation, that is to say, relationships among people, it is important to say that there were no major incidents at the time, as yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, I wonder if you could be given, please, Exhibit P395. In English, it's 395A. I think that's the way that the numbering goes. I'm so sorry. Yes, Ms. Cmeric reminded me. 395A is the Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond transcript, because 395 is the disk, I think. But the registrar, Madam Registrar has it all under control, as always. And then 395A.1 is the English, I think. This is a transcript of apparently a conversation between Mr. Radovan Karadzic and Mr. Slobodan Milosevic, and on the second page of the English, I think we can pick it up, I'm not sure exactly where it is in the B/C/S. But do you see Mr. Milosevic saying: "Yes, yes." "Da, da" probably. Yes. It's about five boxes down on the B/C/S version. Do you see that? I'm just trying to check first whether we've got the right passage, Mr. Bjelobrk. It should be on the second page, about five or six boxes down, Mr. Milosevic is saying: "Yes, yes." Do you see that? Got it? Yes. Thank you. So, I'll just read the box above. Mr. Karadzic says: "No. We said it was in case of breakup of the constitutional system as long as there is --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not sure we referred him to the right "da, da" I think it's the "da da" at the bottom of page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, I think it's elsewhere altogether. My apologies. It's actually on page -- it's on the sixth page of the English, and in fact it's Mr. Radovan Karadzic who would have been saying - Mr. Hannis and I are showing off our B/C/S, Your Honour - "da, da, da." Yes, and it's at the very foot of page 6 of the B/C/S version. So it's three boxes down on page 6 of the English version, and it's at the very foot -- my apologies, Your Honour. We're trying to match the English and the B/C/S. In the B/C/S, page 6, and about four boxes down. There are a couple of blank boxes. It's Mr. Milosevic who says: "Da, da, dobro." Do you have that? So: "Yes, yes, yes" is apparently the translation. Because -- oh, no. "Yes, yes, good." And then: "I think this could pass if they accept this." And then Mr. Milosevic says, and this is the beginning of the passage we heard: "What about Durakovic's men? Well, they are desperate. Did they vote for the Izetbegovic's probably proposals." Is the way it's translated. Just pausing there. Durakovic's men included you, didn't it, Mr. Bjelobrk?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And so Mr. Milosevic says: "Did they vote for Izetbegovic's probably proposals?" Mr. Karadzic said: "No. They left yesterday morning." Mr. Slobodan Milosevic: "Yes." In fact, what had happened was when Mr. Karadzic refers to: "No. They left yesterday morning" was that you, that's to say Mr. Durakovic's men, including yourself, you had left the Assembly, hadn't you?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And Mr. Krajisnik asked you to come back?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Why did you leave the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, when we were proposing to include our proposal into the -- on the agenda, it was refused. We asked for additional discussion on that matter, which was also turned down. And then we left the session because we felt where it was going to take us, that it was going to lead to an ethnic confrontation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, let me make it clear what I'm putting to you. It's not my case on behalf of Mr. Krajisnik, and I'm not putting it to you there was something disgraceful or dishonourable about your leaving the Assembly. What I am putting to you is that members of an assembly or parliament leaving an assembly from time to time when they are serious issues and there are deep tensions is just part of the cut and thrust of politics, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It is not part of the cut and thrust of politics, Mr. Stewart. In the part of the discussion concerning the President of the Court, I would like to clarify this a bit. It is quite natural that at any given session you be given some space to explain your proposal. In this particular situation, it was completely impossible for us to put that proposal on the agenda. Quite another matter is whether they would have voted against it or for it. Secondly, what you mentioned in your earlier question, the tensions existing in the society, we were aware of the fact that such a development would directly lead to a confrontation among the political oligarchies of these national parties, which, as a matter of fact, did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, let's get real. You agree, do you, it's the same, procedurally, in a parliament, it's the same and the same result whether a particular deputy sits there and does nothing and doesn't vote and simply keeps quiet, or whether he leaves, from the point of view of votes and procedures and effects on resolutions, it's exactly the same, isn't it, of course? Isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Technically, you may be right. But I suppose that we are not talking about the technical aspect of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Let's get real. Technically that is clearly right, Mr. Bjelobrk, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not clearly right. I suppose you would like to draw a comparison with my thesis concerning the walkout of the SDS MPs and Mr. Krajisnik's conduct. Well, that's not the same. In this particular case, there was still the possibility of establishing an agenda and of having a democratic option of speaking up. In the case of the SDS members, it was after the adoption of the agenda that they left, and not before, and that's quite different. So if you try to draw a comparison to the two groups of members leaving an assembly, well, it cannot be drawn to that extent. There's a difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Don't worry too much about comparisons, Mr. Bjelobrk, and just concentrate on my questions and answers, please. The -- leaving an assembly by a member or a group of members is simply a political gesture which is stronger than sitting there and not voting, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In this particular case, we were simply struggling to get a chance to speak our minds.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, if you stay there, you can speak your minds, can't you?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because we did not have that item on the agenda, and according to the rules of procedure, the chairman, the Speaker of the parliament, could always tell me that I am not allowed to speak on that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can we get one thing straight, then, and try to short-circuit this as much as possible. Because I, with the greatest respect, Mr. Bjelobrk, I'm going to try to follow entirely His Honour's guidance yesterday that some of these issues we really don't have to get into. Isn't the position this, Mr. Bjelobrk: As really appeared from your evidence, you can point to no occasion on which the rules of procedure and the voting mechanisms in the Bosnia and Herzegovina Assembly were not properly, lawfully, constitutionally operated; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rules of procedure were indeed abided by, and this is something that was really applied properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on, then, Mr. Bjelobrk. You were asked about whether -- it's a related point, but you were asked some questions about whether Mr. Krajisnik had influence or power to make the SDS members that you say had walked out stay there, and then you were asked specifically by His Honour Judge Orie, you were asked whether there was any fact known to you, and this is at page 30 of yesterday's transcript, whether there was any fact known to you which would demonstrate that Mr. Krajisnik was encouraging any of the SDS members to leave. And your answer was: "I don't know anything about that, because the meetings within the clubs," by which you clearly meant the Deputies Clubs, "The meetings with the clubs were usually behind closed doors, and I don't know what went on there." Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond Mr. Bjelobrk, that is beyond the particular context of that question, that is generally true, isn't it? You were not a party to SDS Deputies Club discussions and were not present at any such discussions at all, were you?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never at any of the meetings of the SDS Deputies Club.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And discussions among the SDS leadership, really however we exactly define that is sufficient for the purpose of this question, discussions among the SDS leadership were at all times held behind closed doors in the sense that those doors were closed to you, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I want to ask you about what you described as three stages of the separation of government conducted by the SDS, and that's the way you've described the topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And Your Honour, this particular passage of evidence was at page 45 of yesterday's transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis asked you about paragraphs 26 and 27 of your statement, and I'm going to quote his answer. He said: "Where you describe the SDS as engaging in a parallel process and the formation of parallel structures. Can you" -- it's still Mr. Hannis talking. "Can you tell the Court what evidence, if any, did you see or hear or become aware of in 1991 and early 1992 about the SDS engaging in that process, and give us some examples, if you have some." And your answer was: "I think that there were three stages in terms of this separation of government conducted by the SDS. In the first stage, the beginning of 1991, the assemblies where the SDS was in power were made bigger." And that was corrected, I think, so that it should now read the municipalities where the SDS was in power, were made bigger. And then you said: "Also local officials were instructed to implement the constitution of Yugoslavia, not the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina." And you gave a clarification of what you had said there about municipalities being made bigger. A couple of pages later on, you said: "Well, they weren't made bigger physically. They were instructed that whenever they were supposed to resolve a problem they should resort to the provisions of the Constitution of Yugoslavia rather than the Constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina." That is what the situation was in January 1991, and that's a quote from page 47 of yesterday's transcript. Now, on this point: That instruction to local officials to implement the Constitution of Yugoslavia understood to mean that if there was any conflict between the Constitution of Yugoslavia and the Constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that was an entirely correct instruction, completely in accordance with the law of the state that you were in at that time, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're quite right. You're completely right. If you allow me, I'd like to add some clarification to that. The Constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina was harmonised with the Constitution of Yugoslavia much earlier on, and for many years to come, there were no controversies in terms of the harmonisation of these two constitutions. Secondly, in the area related to the reserve forces and the Territorial Defence units, there were authorities vested in the republic organs, and the then participants in the government, that is, the SDS, HDZ, and the SDA, were actually discussing and debating about which core of the law should be adopted. The SDS gave precedence to the federal law. But I assure that the issue of the harmonisation of the two constitutions was by far the least problem. Evidently, what was the point there was the unification of Serbs only, which had a significant impact on the exercise of the government in Bosnia-Herzegovina. You had such cases, for instance, in the -- among the presidents of the municipalities where the SDS was in power. Because they were the only ones considering this type of a variant. Instead of going through the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, where members of the SDS were also represented, in these -- it was quite natural that such solutions should be discussed at these higher levels of government, and solutions found. Equally so, it is quite unnatural and unlawful for it to be done partially, only in one segment of the government, and that's what I meant in the passage that you quoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, I also just briefly want to make it clear, rather than by a question, but also so that the Trial Chamber, with respect, can understand my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I absolutely am accepting what I understood to be Your Honour's invitation not to explore constitutional law issues, particularly with this witness. And as far as possible, then not very much at all, where they're really not the key issue in the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, you are an experienced and highly qualified man, but you are not, I think we can agree, a constitutional lawyer. So I'm going to leave more of those questions. The -- however, what I am going to ask you about is a passage from the transcript which is P398.

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I be allowed to say a brief comment, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Bjelobrk, I think I'm in His Honour's hands on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, the matters are whether always the right solutions were found or were adopted as far as potential conflicts between the federal constitution and the republic constitutions are concerned is not in the core of this case, so that's, whether right or wrong, it may have been a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And 398, it appears on the transcript as well on page 48 yesterday, but it's probably just easier for everybody if we look at the exhibit itself, and certainly for you, Mr. Bjelobrk, naturally.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: 398, Mr. Koljevic is talking, first page, about four or five -- well, 1, 2, 3, 4 -- not about. Six boxes down Mr. Koljevic says: "Tell me something. Has the law proposed by the government to suspend the federal law been adopted?" Do you see that box, Mr. Bjelobrk?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic: "Yes, at the government level. At the government level, it was --" Mr. Koljevic: "Did the Assembly" -- he was going to say it was "adopt" something or other. Mr. Koljevic: "Did the assembly adopt it too?" Mr. Karadzic: "No, no. The Assembly is the Board of Citizens. The Board of Municipalities rejected it earlier and whatever the Board of Citizens does now, it would not be valid. No one has the right to do that and nobody will. It has not been adopted and our municipalities will not obey it. They report to Doko on a regular basis." Mr. Koljevic: "Has it been adopted at the Assembly?" Mr. Karadzic: "No, it hasn't." Mr. Koljevic: "Okay. That's the most important." Mr. Karadzic: "No, it hasn't. And also, our municipalities are not acting according to it."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOLJEVIC
utterances.text: "Okay, then." Now, two things, Mr. Bjelobrk. This is an example of something which, would you agree, was a quite common feature of the political situation in 1991 - this was August 1991 - that there were debates and disagreements about whether something was or wasn't constitutional, whether one party was acting constitutionally. Those were a constant feature of political debate and discussion at that time, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was one of the features.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And that in this particular instance, you can see that the -- would you agree, the point of view being adopted by Mr. Karadzic was that, in fact, the proposal to suspend the federal law had not been adopted anyway? That's clearly what he's saying, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'll make it clear. Yes. In this conversation between Mr. Koljevic and Mr. Karadzic, what is emerging is that the suspension of the federal law has been approved or adopted by the government, but has not been approved or adopted by the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That's what it's saying, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And it's also clear that Mr. Koljevic and Mr. Karadzic, particularly, are taking the view that if it were adopted, that wouldn't be valid and lawful anyway. That's plainly also what they're saying, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will tell you what I think about this, and keeping in mind what you and the honourable President said here. There are institutions --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Tell us first, Mr. Bjelobrk, whether you agree that that is what these gentlemen who are parties to this conversation are saying.

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to the transcript, that was your interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, I'm inviting your agreement that whether you think they're right or not, that is clearly what they're saying.

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a document of the Court. Yes, that's what it says, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And based -- what is happening here is based on their view that this suspension of the federal law has not actually been validly adopted, and even if it had purportedly been adopted, it wouldn't be valid. Based on that view, they are also saying between themselves that their municipalities wouldn't obey and won't obey such a suspension of federal law. That's also what they're saying, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking my opinion about it or are you asking me for the third time whether this is what this paper before me says?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I am asking you for the third time, on a third and different point, Mr. Bjelobrk. Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I think about this. An assessment as to whether a piece of legislation conforms with the constitution is something to be done by members of the legal profession rather than the general public or the politicians discussing about the substance of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, Mr. Stewart is asking you whether you understand this conversation to be that Mr. Koljevic and Mr. Karadzic discuss whether a law proposed by the government to suspend the federal law has been adopted or not, that the answer is that it was not adopted, and even if it would have been adopted, that they would not have accepted that as something they would obey. Is that your understanding of this conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's how I understood this conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's clear now, Mr. Stewart. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, you'd agree with this, wouldn't you: That if leading figures - and I'm certainly not going to resile from suggesting that Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Koljevic were leading figures - if leading figures in a political party take the view that an action of another group, another party, the government, is unconstitutional and unlawful, it's a perfectly understandable and natural consequence that they would instruct their colleagues and instruct their municipalities, which is the way they describe it, not to obey. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree. I think that whatever is unlawful should be approved or disapproved by the president of the republic or the president of the Assembly, because they are vested with these authorities. I don't think that this is something to be done by the leaders of a political party. That is not the way matters are run in a state when deciding on these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I feel I've gone far enough on this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- in your statement, this was, and I don't think for the moment, Mr. Bjelobrk, you would be unfairly disadvantaged by -- I'll be disadvantaged by throwing my transcript on the floor. But I don't think you'll be unfairly disadvantaged by not having the actual text in front of you, Mr. Bjelobrk. You refer to a meeting in respect of the Belgrade Initiative, which I don't think was explored in your oral evidence in chief. But describe in a nutshell for us, Mr. Bjelobrk, your summary of the Belgrade Initiative.

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Belgrade Initiative is one of the attempts at formulating a Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The Belgrade Initiative came, not surprisingly, as its name implies, it came primarily from the Serb leadership in Belgrade, under Mr. Milosevic, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the context from which it stemmed. It could have stemmed from Visegrad or Sarajevo. But it does merit the qualification that I just mentioned earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I rather, from your statement, Mr. Bjelobrk, when you said: "Further discussions in respect of this proposal took place in September, October 1991, and at that time the SDS acted as a mediator between the SDA and Belgrade authorities. The people who triggered this Belgrade Initiative were people coming from Belgrade." I rather inferred from that, Mr. Bjelobrk, and therefore would invite you to reconsider, that the Belgrade Initiative did come primarily from the Serb leadership in Belgrade. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you need an answer, yes, they were the authors. But you asked what my characterisation of that document was, regardless of where it originated from.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, so you say in your statement that the SDS acted as a mediator between the SDA and Belgrade authorities. The essence of the Belgrade Initiative was that it, in effect, accepted the writing on the wall that Slovenia and Croatia would at some point leave federal Yugoslavia, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was one of the positions contained in the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And another essential element of the Belgrade Initiative was that Bosnia and Herzegovina would remain with the other three republics, if you take away Slovenia and Croatia, would remain within a single state of Yugoslavia; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That's what the document said as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Beyond -- and those were, would you agree, Mr. Bjelobrk, those were the key elements of the Belgrade Initiative?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would perhaps add another one, although I do agree that the ones that you mentioned are among the key elements. But there are others that I would point out. For instance, the position of the Muslims in this union, in this association, and that was the key to the understanding of the participants taking part in this particular discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Bjelobrk, I invite you to do pretty much what you've just suggested, because it will helpfully answer a question I asked a few minutes ago. So if we take those as you acknowledge that those two elements of Slovenia and Croatia at some point ceasing to be part of Yugoslavia but Bosnia and Herzegovina and the other three republics remaining within Yugoslavia, if those are not necessarily in order priority in our view, but if those are number 1, number 2, I'm inviting you to add to that what, in your view, what are the other key elements of the Belgrade Initiative. Perhaps number them as we go along and then we'll be clear which they are.

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have this document in front of me now, so I'm speaking from my memory. I do agree that the two important elements were the ones that you mentioned. But in my opinion, the element concerning the position of the Muslims in this particular association was another important element. As for the rest, I don't think it was as important when talking about the documents at this particular level.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right. That's helpful, Mr. Bjelobrk, certainly. So then going to that other key element that you mentioned, then, concerning -- that's quotes, concerning the position of the Muslims in this particular association, can you expand a little bit on that, then? What was that element of the Belgrade Initiative, so far as the Muslims were concerned?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document in its form of a proposal - you know that the document was never really finalised - there was one provision where the Muslims were guaranteed a certain group of rights in this particular social association. I can merely give you my opinion on it. And that's where, in -- essentially Bosnia and Herzegovina was misunderstood, because its constitutive nations started being treated as if they weren't really the constituent elements of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So pulling out of that answer a specifically the point relating to the Muslims, it was -- there was a guarantee of a -- what you describe as a certain group of rights for the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What is it that specifically that leads you to characterise the Belgrade Initiative, then, as the establishment of a Greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, physically speaking, it mentions the territories where the Serbs have the majority or wished to be in control of. So there is no Croatia there, there is no Slovenia. It was an idea of Greater Serbia, mentioning -- ending, actually, with the border running across Karlobag, Karlovac. This was not an idea for a Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, I assure the Trial Chamber, I don't wish to engage in unnecessarily wide exploration of history and politics, but this simple element to the background applies, doesn't it: That Belgrade, Serbia, the Serb leadership in Belgrade, they didn't expel and weren't interested in expelling Slovenia and Croatia from Yugoslavia, were they?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that, although I'm not prepared to agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The initiative for Slovenia and Croatia to leave Yugoslavia came from Slovenia and Croatia, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you think that there is some kind of bureaucratic way of putting it, if we're only talking about a particular piece of paper or a statement, whatever, then you may be right, but there's so many things that happened over a span of ten years or so that contributed to the actual outcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there something sinister about the Belgrade Initiative, in your view, Mr. Bjelobrk?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sinister? If I look at the Helsinki Final Act on the inviolability of borders in Europe, then indeed the Belgrade declaration was sinister, because it contributed to a change of internal and external borders, compared to what they were like before.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what change do you mean there?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, if I can put it this way, the Belgrade authorities played a role that contributed to the change of the external borders of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You mean the departure or imminent departure of Slovenia and Croatia from the Federation, do you?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Of course. I'm convinced, confident. I have arguments to prove that it is the Belgrade authorities that are responsible for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So is --

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also -- may I just finish, please. Also, ultimately to attempting to change interior borders as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, I tried to keep it as simple and as short as possible. If I understand your answer, you have just characterised as a sinister element of the Belgrade Initiative as it led to redrawing of the external borders of Yugoslavia by the loss or exclusion of Slovenia and Croatia. That's a correct summary of what you just said, is it?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am going to give up on terms like "sinister" and whatever as you did on the first day. So I'll try to stick to the facts. The Belgrade Initiative is one of the events, one of the elements, that contributed to the further breakup of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: On the footing, and that has to be the basis of this proposition, Mr. Bjelobrk, on the footing that Croatia and Slovenia were going to leave Yugoslavia at some point in some way or another, the Belgrade Initiative preserved the rest of Yugoslavia as fully as could be, didn't it? Or would have done, rather.

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My position is that that was the creation of a Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, we've entered in quite some detail in political analysis rather than anything else. If you would ask a woman why she left the house, she will always say that her husband made her do that and the husband will always say that he only wants to keep his family together. And as you know from normal life, that it's very difficult there to assess exactly what is the truth, what is the causal relationship. It very much depends again on the analysis and opinion on what happened. I think we very much entered into this area. The positions are quite clear that this witness, Mr. Bjelobrk, blames certain initiatives for things that happened later. And I think it's for historians to finally deal with that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm very happy with that, Your Honour. In fact, I really was culminating with one question specifically on a point in his statement which ought to wrap up this topic, which is this, Mr. Bjelobrk.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In your statement, at paragraph 28, then, in relation to all this issue, you said: "The concept of preservation of Yugoslavia was utilised by the Serbian leadership as a veil for this policy," meaning the policy of Greater Serbia. Now, Mr. Bjelobrk, when you say "a veil," that is, do you agree, that is implying something secret, sinister, devious, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'll try to steer clear of these attributes and give you an answer nevertheless. The country to the east of Bosnia-Herzegovina is now called Serbia and Montenegro. Before that it was called Yugoslavia. And it grew out of the Yugoslavia that existed in the 1980s. That particular development probably proves best of all that this was only a veil for a Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not proposing to pursue this any more, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, in relation of paragraph 28, it reads that the document which is dated 12th of August, and then a few lines later it says: "Further discussions in respect of this proposal took place in September, October 1991." Reconciling this, I'm -- is that a wrong reading, wrong understanding, of what this paragraph says or...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. Well, Your Honour's just read the very words that are in the paragraph. I'm not -- I'm sorry. Maybe I'm being a bit thick, Your Honour. I'm not following Your Honour's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It says: "August 1991, the initial meeting in respect of the Belgrade Initiative took place. I have been shown a document. This document is dated 12th of August." And then if the "further," a few lines later, is in relation to the August 1991 initial meeting, then I do understand it. If the "further" is in relation to the 12th of August, 1992 document, I have some difficulties in following the chronology. It's just --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, I'm so sorry, Your Honour. I see the -- I see the point. I'm afraid I'd not noticed it. I rather suppose -- but perhaps you could confirm, Mr. Bjelobrk. I suspect 1992 is simply a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think what Mr. Stewart has just said is correct. We should confirm with the witness. But I believe that is a typo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I was just going to confirm with the witness, Your Honour. Sometimes what happens is it's so obviously in a sense should be 1991 that your brain reads it as 1991 and that's what I'd done. I hadn't even noticed the discrepancy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, in the -- I hope you can manage without the statement. In your statement, and I'll read two or three lines slowly, as I'm always being reminded to do anyway, it says: "In August 1991, the initial meeting in respect of the Belgrade Initiative took place." And it plainly was 1991. We can all agree that: "I have been shown a document." Reference number. "In this document dated 12th of August..." and it says 1992, "...the basic Serb position is set out including the fact that the preservation of Yugoslavia is a condition for a peaceful and democratic solution to the Yugoslav crisis." Mr. Bjelobrk, it appears to all of us, and we invite you to confirm that that reference to the document being dated 12th of August, 1992, it should be to the 12th of August, 1991. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. I'd simply not noticed that discrepancy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- then, Mr. Bjelobrk, in your evidence yesterday, and this is page 52 of the transcript, for the reference, you were asked by Mr. Hannis -- I'll quote the question. He says: "Now, in your statement, where you talk in paragraphs 26 and 27 about the parallel process, you also talked about regionalisation, which I think is what you referred to in an earlier answer in talking about the creation of the Serb Autonomous Regions. Do you recall when that first became public knowledge or in the awareness of the public that there was any kind of formal media announcement about those Serb Autonomous Regions?" And your answer was: "The public was formally informed only at the moment when these forms of regionalisation, as they termed them in the SDS, were formally established. The second aspect of it is that many of these notions did emerge in the press in the independent media; therefore, my direct answer to your question would be the following: There were no official, formal announcements of these acts, but by interpreting the different discussions that went on between various politicians, like, for instance, something that we heard in the penultimate transcript, and of course this reached the Assembly members, and we could infer our own conclusions. Thirdly, I was born and I live in Sarajevo; however, many of my colleagues live in other areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina. They directly conveyed to me the information as to what was going on in their communities. That was sufficient information for me to be indirectly informed about all these processes." Now, that's a slightly lengthy passage, but I wanted to remind you of what you said. Mr. Bjelobrk, the -- whatever the formal position, it's very clear, isn't it, that this process, however you characterise it, but process on one label of regionalisation, creation of Serb Autonomous Regions, it was not some secret process which could possibly be kept from public knowledge, was it?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course it could not have been kept from public knowledge, but it was illegal nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure exactly what time we started, but if that would be a convenient time for a break. It's not -- I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Due to technical difficulties, we started a bit late, but it is the usual time we have a break. So we'll have a break until 10 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I ask straight away, I mentioned to Mr. Hannis, I wonder if the Trial Chamber would be willing to give me, and it is me, a five-minute break at a quarter to 5.00. The reason is just that there are certain practical matters which can't be dealt with tomorrow because it's a holiday and can't be dealt with unless they're sorted out by 5.00 this evening. And I wasn't able to resolve them over the recent break, most of which I spent with Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Five minutes will be granted. If you could look at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you very much, indeed, Your Honour. I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, you referred in your statement, this is, to -- well, no. It's actually in your evidence. The -- but also in your statement. This was page 57 and onwards of the transcript yesterday. And I'll summarise. It's really what you have described as a difference between Mr. Krajisnik's public persona and the way in which he acted and spoke in private. You recall that passage of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, it's -- you're an experienced politician. It's 100 per cent normal, isn't it, for there to be differences between the way in which politicians present themselves to the public through the media and the way in which they have private discussions with their colleagues and/or opponents?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps it's not right for me to start by giving myself as an example, but I behave the same way in my public life and in private life, and I'm sure that there are many other politicians who do the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You've seen a lot of them, have you, Mr. Bjelobrk, politicians who behave just the same in public as they do in private?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I had the good fortune of meeting Mr. Pertini, for example, a top-notch politician in Italy, many others in Europe, and I never managed to discern any differences between the conversations they had in private and what they said to the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of course, perhaps, Mr. Bjelobrk, you've met politicians who behave the same in public and in private and are therefore never used as media spokesmen, have you?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I understood your question correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Never mind, Mr. Bjelobrk. I'll withdraw it. Let's cut to the chase with Mr. Krajisnik. Is there -- was there anything objectionable about the way Mr. Krajisnik acted and spoke and dealt with you and others in your presence in private?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I'm not complaining about anything. I remember that the President of the Court also used an expression, possible political games. I'm just saying that people who got to know Mr. Krajisnik as a person found out before the general public what his intentions actually were, and I tried to explain that by using the example of the interview he gave in January 1992. Some politicians had this knowledge and came to learn about this even before January 1992, whereas the public did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You had a meeting with Mr. Krajisnik that you describe at paragraph 32 of your statement, and you gave some evidence about it. You had a meeting -- you say it's March 1992, and a conversation which involved Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Lazovic. Remember that?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And who was -- was anybody else present in addition to yourself, Mr. Krajisnik, and Mr. Lazovic?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that meeting, there were only the three of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you said that, in your statement, this is, at paragraph 32, you said Mr. Krajisnik: "Referred to Serb intellectuals, claiming that they themselves could not live with the other nationalities in the same country." Mr. Krajisnik didn't, in fact, agree with the Serb intellectuals group that he referred to, did he?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not my understanding that Mr. Krajisnik disagreed with these Serb intellectuals. On the contrary; one of his questions was: Why would we not join this meeting of Serb intellectuals that was taking place at the Holiday Inn hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's a different question, Mr. Bjelobrk. It was not Mr. Krajisnik's expressed view, was it, that the -- that the three nationalities - Serbs, Muslims, Croats - could not live together in the same country, was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we have a date on --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, yes. The date, I believe, was March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The date was given as March 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It wasn't Mr. Krajisnik's expressed view, was it, Mr. Bjelobrk?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that he then mentioned the position of the Serb intellectuals, as he had put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, that's not answering my question. I'll put it the third time, Mr. Bjelobrk. It wasn't Mr. Krajisnik's expressed view, was it, that the three nationalities could not live together in the same country?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that meeting, that was not the subject of that meeting. I mentioned it in the statement. The first was our attitude towards the meetings of Serb intellectuals, and the second, why we did not support the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Let's be very specific, then, Mr. Bjelobrk. At that meeting, Mr. Krajisnik did not express the view that the three nationalities could not live together in the same country, did he?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You referred to another meeting, a completely different meeting, completely different topic, as you described it, when you had occasion to go and speak to Mr. Krajisnik about a financial problem, and you described it: There was a problem. You were the president of a trade union in Sarajevo, and there was some money due from -- in a nutshell, there was some money due from Belgrade to Sarajevo. That was -- that's a fair shorthand description, isn't it? And it was $50 million. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what was it that -- what was it that Mr. Krajisnik, if anything, what was Mr. Krajisnik being invited to do or help with in relation to that issue?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We expected the prime minister and the president of the Assembly to help us establish contact with the authorities in Belgrade; that is to say, the authorities that were in charge of the company that had this outstanding debt of $50 million. I assumed that it was quite understandable. We were interested in it to the degree to which it affected the workers' wages and salaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did you get the help that you were seeking?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not get this help from the president of the Assembly, and from the government bodies, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What was it specifically, if anything, what was it, then, that you were specifically asking from Mr. Krajisnik that you didn't get?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We asked for a meeting to be arranged for us in Belgrade with the persons in charge of that problem, and also transportation to Belgrade, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you asked Mr. Krajisnik to arrange that, did you?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not for him to arrange it directly, but to vest his authority in it; namely, to ask the persons who could do it to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And do you say he failed to do what you asked him to do?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the matter was satisfactorily resolved, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The same evening, the federal government intervened and the money was paid to the Sarajevo company. If you're interested in details, there was a meeting in Belgrade, at 4.00 in the afternoon. A flight was scheduled before that, and in the evening, the money had been paid out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And was there something -- anything objectionable about Mr. Krajisnik's conduct at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my statement, I gave my view of his behaviour at the meeting that we had with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, forgot about your statement. Well, not forget about it, but just answer my question, please, Mr. Bjelobrk. Was there anything objectionable about Mr. Krajisnik's conduct at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've said that he raised the issue of who does not like Belgrade, for instance. And we did not come to discuss that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: How did that come up, the issue of who does not like Belgrade? Mr. Bjelobrk, something must have provoked some such comment. How did that come up?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You'd probably have to ask Mr. Krajisnik that, why he said it. I'm just telling you. So the only provocation from our side was that there was this debt that was owed a particular company, and we insisted that the government help us we solve this. Basically this is no provocation, and it should not lead to any kind of discussion as to who likes what or dislikes what.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, you see, I'm asking you, Mr. Bjelobrk, because you're the one who remembers this meeting and says you were at the meeting. That's the reason I'm asking you questions. So are you saying you can't remember how the question of who dislikes Belgrade came up? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember very well that this question was raised by Mr. Krajisnik, and I've said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. But do you remember, Mr. Bjelobrk, what it was that gave rise to that question by Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, now the witness has answered this question I think two or three times. He said we raised the issue of a debt still outstanding to be paid. And Mr. Krajisnik said: Are you against Belgrade? That's at least how I understand the testimony. But if I'm wrong, Mr. Bjelobrk, please tell me. That's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have understood me properly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Witnesses always say that the Judge has understood the testimony correctly. We've hardly had a single example of that not happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart. Mr. Stewart, you have asked this question a couple of times. I asked the question yesterday how the issue came up. And he repeatedly answered the question by saying that the matter was raised by Mr. Krajisnik when they had raised the issue of the outstanding debt. And that's a clear answer and you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honour, he hasn't answered it clearly. When I gave --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, we can look on the record what he said, Your Honour, and what he didn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You referred to the National Equality Council, Mr. Bjelobrk, and you said that in your opinion this idea of creating this exclusive body was simply a way of trying to discuss the matters of ethnic equality in a narrow -- among a narrow circle of people. Mr. Bjelobrk, are you implying or is it your view that there was something improperly manipulative about the setting up of this body?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I wanted to say, and I think I managed to explain it: There was this Presidency which comprised two representatives from each of the ethnicities and one from the ranks of others. And they had the constitutional and legal authorities to discuss all the issues related to ethnic equality. Similarly, there was such a situation in the Assembly as well. There were bodies there vested with the authority to discuss and decide upon the issues relating to ethnic equality. The council was established nearly with an advisory role, therefore, to advise the bodies in their decision-taking process. I agree with those [indiscernible] who said that at the time, this was not a proper way of dealing with the then existing problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you say that the body was, in your opinion, too narrow? Too narrow a circle?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not the most important point I was trying to make, whether this was a narrow or in a larger circle. The issue of ethnic equality basically came up from those who were vested with the authority of taking decisions. In practice, very often we would, in cases where there would be unsolved issues at the Presidency or in the parliament, those issues that related to ethnic equality that were left unsolved would then be forwarded to the council for ethnic equality.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm just trying to get clear, Mr. Bjelobrk. Is it your position that what you have told the Trial Chamber about the National Equality Council is intended to be descriptive but not critical in any way of the composition and functioning of that body?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wanted to point out that the very point of their existing a council for such matters showed that both the Presidency and the Assembly had not functioned properly, because they had to wait, whether it was justified or unjustified, they had to wait for a conclusion to be taken at that body.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, wasn't the underlying idea behind that body precisely to try to sort out some of these issues in a smaller group -- well, in a smaller group rather than simply have them brought into the Assembly without that considered prior review?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've interpreted this idea of this particular body properly. Unfortunately, this body became an obstacle in the way of solving this, these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Because there was disagreement within the body itself?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You referred to an article in the publication called Oslobodjenje, and this is dealt with at paragraph 55 of your statement. It was dealt with very briefly in evidence, at page 97 of the transcript. But, Your Honour, the witness effectively just referred back to paragraph 55 of his statement, so it wasn't pursued any further specifically in oral evidence. I'm just finding it, Your Honour. Not strictly accurate. I'm trying to find it, Your Honour. That's a more correct way of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps already for your guidance, Mr. Stewart, the article, Oslobodjenje, of course, has been tendered into evidence, and apart from a short summary of what an interview says, the Chamber rather will look at the interview itself, and if it reads the same in the interview as the witness did, fine; if not, then the Chamber will certainly rely on its own reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You make a number of comments in your statement, Mr. Bjelobrk, about the points in the article. And I'm looking --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think here it would be appropriate for the witness to have the B/C/S version of his statement. I don't think it would be fair to him not to have it in front of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if, given that it's coming up to a quarter to, and it will take me a few minutes, Your Honour's kind agreement that I might have five minutes, I wonder if this would be the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll grant you five minutes. We'll adjourn until 10 minutes to 5.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you very much. --- Break taken at 4.43 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart. You managed to make your phone call.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you very much. I'd just like to say: I did sort out what I wanted to sort out and I wouldn't have been able to without the break. So I do appreciate that very much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, I was asking to ask you, and am asking you, about this article: "We are from the Balkans, after all," which is -- it's Exhibit P404. You'll need the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it, Mr. Stewart, that a part which is not translated which seems to say that it's an interview with Mr. Krajisnik, because that doesn't appear in the translation, I see it on the photograph, that's one. There's no disagreement between the parties that this is an interview with Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it's an article based on an interview with Mr. Krajisnik. There's no disagreement about it being Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But it even says so, as far as I can --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. No, Your Honour is quite right. It does actually on the original, there's even a picture of him. We don't see that here. So there's no question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Second very short observation. If you would look at page 5 of the English text, the question appears: "And why don't the Serbs want to live in an independent BiH? If you would look in the original, it seems rather to be a question Mr. Krajisnik puts to himself than a question that has been put to him by the interviewer. In the original, it's the -- almost at the top of the fourth column. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then if that's understood by everyone, then we don't need to have a redacted version. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It was -- I hope it won't cause a problem. I understand that the copy Mr. Krajisnik's working from is still not easy, but he's just about managing. But no doubt he'll tell us if he runs into problem. Your Honour, I have a slight problem, which is I don't know what's happened to my headphones. I've got the wrong headphones on probably. I've got the wrong ones on. That's the simple solution to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Right, Mr. Bjelobrk. You, in your statement, you make a number of points in relation to this particular article or interview, and you say your reaction was negative and then you give the reasons why your reaction was negative. You first of all say that Mr. Krajisnik states that it's impossible for Bosnia and Herzegovina to remain, the word in English, unitarian, when Yugoslavia disintegrates. You say he is setting an ultimatum in respect of the fate of Bosnia and Herzegovina based on his own national or political ideas. And it is true that what Mr. Krajisnik says in translation is: It is impossible -- or is reported as saying: It is impossible for Bosnia to remain unitary - is probably a better word - if Yugoslavia disintegrates. Mr. Bjelobrk, that was not an uncommon view, was it, at that time?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, it was unusual, although it was not the only such a public statement, but it was unusual in terms of the normal civilisational outlook.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, you've no reason, have you, to suppose it wasn't an honest view of Mr. Krajisnik's?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no such reason, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And when you say he's setting an ultimatum, where do you find an ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under item 55.6, I describe the explanation to a question. If we have a war or a dramatic transformation there, then that constitutes an ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Well, thank you for that clarification. Yes, you see, I was just looking for somewhere different from 55.6, but that's at the top of page 3 of the English version, more or less at the very top, where he says: "Now" -- or is reported as saying: "Now we are left with two alternatives: Either war or a" -- no word "dramatic" there, actually, as there was in your answer. But: "Either war or a transformation that implies an agreement between the three national communities." Now, that, Mr. Bjelobrk, is expressed there, and I put it to you that was the position, that it wasn't an ultimatum; it was Mr. Krajisnik's assessment of the situation. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can call it the way you want. I will try to explain to you, because I'm a person who lived in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I think you live in a similar country. When you look at the way the population in Bosnia and Herzegovina was mixed, there is very little space for a one dominant ethnic population or a mono-ethnic community. Any type of an agreement that you've been alluding to implies the movement of certain peoples, willingly or forcibly. And I don't think it comes under the category of ideas, as you put it, that you could simply place on a table.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, isn't the position this, Mr. Bjelobrk: That as things were - this is January 1992 - that it was a widespread view that Bosnia and Herzegovina couldn't simply remain the way it was?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not under the impression that this was a widespread view. I don't want to take up your time.
