You had the analysis by the international community and their conclusions, and you will see that matters were not the way you say. The internal, political climate in Bosnia-Herzegovina was such that you had one group who were in favour of the transformation of the internal structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but with the -- under the same name. So I cannot really agree with you that this was a widespread view.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, are you -- I don't want to go into it in great detail, but are you -- you know about and are to some extent familiar with the discussions in relation to the Cutileiro Plan, are you?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was partly familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And Cutileiro Plan didn't simply contemplate status quo, did it?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did not contemplate a status quo, but as far as I understood it, it did not divide Bosnia and Herzegovina only along the ethnic lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There were public statements by representatives of other nationalities, weren't there, which expressly recognised the possibility of war?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must admit that I cannot remember the specific statements right now, other than those that came from the SDS. I recall others speaking up on those lines. Somewhere around February 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you remember that as far back as February 1991, Mr. Izetbegovic had said, and I'm trying to quote as accurately as I can, but that he would sacrifice peace for sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but he wouldn't sacrifice the sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina for peace? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your second point in your statement 55.2, you say: "Mr. Krajisnik states that it is inevitable to distinguish between the three national communities in Bosnia and Herzegovina and that the Assembly of the Serb People did not want to express it out loud." You say: "This infers that whatever the SDS had done previously was leading to the distinguishing of the three national communities, yet they had not wanted to reveal this." Now, Mr. Bjelobrk, looking at what Mr. Krajisnik is reported as saying, and this is under the second heading, isn't it, the -- do you want to confirm this, under the heading "The formation of the republic of Serb people in BH has caused much criticism." It's that passage, isn't it, and over the page in the English version. But it's that passage that you're referring to here, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can be assisted. I have this version in very small print, and even if I have my glasses, I cannot work this out. Could I perhaps get another version of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a slightly larger version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you could provide it to Mr. Bjelobrk. Mr. Bjelobrk, your attention is drawn to what I would say is the answer to the second question, the questions being underlined. Otherwise, Mr. Stewart, you could read it in English, if the witness is not able to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, then, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then be translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It is pretty small, I think. The passage says: "It was declared as a" -- well, the question was: "Can you explain to us how it's envisaged in a constitutional legal sense - that's the Republic of the Serb People - that is, what its borders are and how authority would be successfully set up in it." And the reported answer: "It was declared as a consequence, that is, as an expression of the desire of the Serb people to remain within the single state of Yugoslavia, together with Serbia and Montenegro, the SAO Krajina, and other Serb areas. It is certain that this move was a reaction to moves made by the two national communities in BH, the illegally voted memorandum and the platform, as well as the illegal and unconstitutional submission of a request for the recognition of the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is something the public is already familiar with, and there are two reasons why many people are not sure about what the Republic of the Serb People of Bosnia-Herzegovina means. We did not want to say this out loud because the Assembly of the Serb People feel that a certain demarcation of the three national communities in Bosnia and Herzegovina is inevitable. A Muslim, a Croat, and a Serb Bosnia will be formed as a result of the demarcation; however, in no case will one state be formed at the expense of another. The second reason lies in the fact that many people who had access to the explanation of what the Republic of the Serb People in Bosnia-Herzegovina meant did not take it seriously enough, and it should be clear to them that this is a very serious move of the Serb people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, one that was forced upon them. It is an invitation to have a Muslim and a Croat Bosnia-Herzegovina also formed."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, would you agree, Mr. Bjelobrk, that, first of all, the reported answer from Mr. Krajisnik there is saying that, quite clearly, that none of the nationalities are to have precedence or priority or dominance over any of the others?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll tell you what I think about this. If Mr. Krajisnik is insisting on a Bosnian Croat and Serb Bosnia-Herzegovina, then already you have the -- this idea coming through, through this nominalisation of the three peoples. Second: Unfortunately, Bosnia and Herzegovina is a country which, in terms of its territory, has a very mixed population. If -- you've probably heard that prior to the war, almost a third of the marriages were mixed with husbands and wives coming from different ethnic backgrounds. And this idea would actually come across a problem even on the example of a one high-rise building where you want to distinguish between peoples of different ethnicities. If this idea were applied to a mono-ethnic country, then it could reasonably be implemented. But in a country like Bosnia and Herzegovina, where over 80 per cent of the territory is occupied by a very mixed population, such an idea would imply the resettlement of people, be it willing or forceful, and that's why I said that nobody reasonable could have advocated such an idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When he's talking about the -- well, your next point, 55.4, where Mr. Krajisnik -- the question is: "Could you specify its borders." And your comment there in your statement is: "Krajisnik describes the borderlines of the republic in terms of where Serbs have established autonomous regions, where they are in a majority, and areas where they were in a majority prior to the genocide committed against them during the last war." And that's -- for all practical purposes, Mr. Bjelobrk, I'm acknowledging that that's an accurate statement of what's in the article immediately under the heading "Could you specifies its borders." And then you go on to make your comments: "They would like to remodel history," et cetera, et cetera. What you miss out there, do you agree, is a sentence which I'll read in English. It's five or six lines down under the heading "Could you specify its borders." "The exact demarcation is, however, not defined. It is a matter of agreement between the three national communities in which the areas and territories would be determined." And you agree that that's omitted from your brief summary, 55.4 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Physically, it was left out; however, I consider it irrelevant. The controversial point was independence. Now, how you implement it, that's a secondary matter. I was here talking about the whole thesis and not the way of implementing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So it's your position that it is irrelevant that Mr. Krajisnik, in the middle of this reported answer, expressly states that the exact demarcation is to be a matter of agreement between the three national communities?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's quite irrelevant to me who the participants to the potential agreement are. In my opinion, this sort of a proposal is contrary to any civilisational heritage that we might have and to any democratic procedures.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And in your next point, 55.5, the way you put it is: "He" - that's Mr. Krajisnik - "...states that at one time they were not at the stage to break up Bosnia-Herzegovina. Implicitly he was stating that whilst before he had not expressed their will to break Bosnia and Herzegovina apart, he was now willing to do so." And you get that, Mr. Bjelobrk, I take it, from the last two or three lines under the heading "Could you specify its borders," where it says: "These are administrative borders that would simply create conditions in which the Serb people would be their own bosses, just as the Muslim and the Croat people, only certain functions would be unitary for the entire Bosnia-Herzegovina. In that sense, there was a desire not to break up Bosnia and Herzegovina but to transform it. Bosnia and Herzegovina must not in any case be subjugated to any republics or states. Mr. Bjelobrk, I do put to you that to infer from that passage in the context of this whole article that Mr. Krajisnik was saying that previously he and the SDS had not wished to break Bosnia and Herzegovina apart but were now willing to do so, is simply a misreading of the interview and the article.

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to briefly explain that you understand -- misunderstand the context of the whole matter. Because for several hundred years, Bosnia and Herzegovina was not just the sum total of three ethnic ghettos. And any option of dividing it does not boil down to the division of some imaginary three ethnic ghettos. You actually have to step into people's apartments. And at that point, this whole process has nothing to do with democracy any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can we get this clear, Mr. Bjelobrk. What we're talking about is your assessment and your view that what Mr. Krajisnik and the SDS had in mind was simply impossible to achieve; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not only that it was impossible to achieve. First of all, the war proved that you can force people to do all sorts of things with weapons. If you're talking about possible and impossible. But we're not talking about that. We're talking about the question of human rights. If you are giving rise to a political idea, the question is whether you are allowing the exercise of human rights or not. I do agree with you here that I'm not a lawyer here or an interpreter of the constitution, but this is an elementary thing, that you should not destroy the level of human rights attained so far. If you would do anything along these lines, you would infringe upon the human rights already enjoyed by the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you agree, Mr. Bjelobrk, that quite a lot of energy, time, by a number of people, to put it mildly, in relation to the international negotiations in 1991 and during early 1992 and later, were devoted precisely to some form of transformation of Bosnia and Herzegovina in order to enable the three nationalities to live with each other within the same state?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And that the transformation which was contemplated in the course of many of those international discussions did involve quite radical changes which would involve some form of entities attributable to the different nationalities?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But if you allow me to say this. Not a single international participant in these processes of seeking solutions said that one of the solutions was war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In paragraph 53 of your statement, you say in your work in the Assembly, you drew the conclusion that Krajisnik was consulted by the deputies of the SDS about all issues. "Whenever disputes were likely to arise in the parliament, the deputies of the SDS would address Krajisnik for an answer, even though the chief of the club was the person they should turn to." Mr. Bjelobrk, can you give a single illustration for us of such a dispute to which the -- on which the deputies of the SDS addressed Mr. Krajisnik for an answer?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I myself asked SDS deputies about some of their statements, for instance, with which I could not agree or where I sought additional clarification. I asked them what kind of support they had within the SDS club, and I checked whether it had been agreed upon with the head of the club, and so on. And very often, the answer I got was that it had been agreed upon with Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So please, Mr. Bjelobrk, if you can, give an example.

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, the discussion of the two memorandums. Of course, by the very nature of things, you talk to people whose views differ from your own. And then I checked the hierarchy to see how these positions were formed, whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, I think I'm going to have to stop you and ask you to be a bit -- we do have memorandums coming outs of our ears in this case. Which memorandums are you talking about now?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a participant in the debate only about two groups of materials, those that were discussed during the summer session of the Assembly and those that were discussed during the autumn session of the Assembly. So I'm talking about the debates concerning these documents, and then I had the opportunity of realising, after having talked to SDS deputies whose views differed from my own, that this position had been developed within the SDS club and that Krajisnik also backed those views.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You've changed the description from the two memorandums to "these documents," Mr. Bjelobrk, which doesn't actually really help us all that much. Which two documents are you talking about, please?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that you have before you the minutes of the October session, and I'll try to jog my memory now. In October, a document was supposed to be looked at, and it was entitled "Memorandum." And then another document that was entitled "Platform." I think that a third document of the SDS was being prepared then. I can't remember the title. In the summer of 1991, the SDA offered a memorandum. The SDP offered a separate text which was called the memorandum, and I think there was also an additional resolution, but all of this can be checked in the minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say, this, I'm afraid, is exactly the sort of area I simply cannot pursue this afternoon because I have to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, what's the problem here? Let's try to -- from what you asked the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour -- I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does it say -- but perhaps I first ask a small question to the witness. If a SDS deputy would speak with the other deputies or with the president of the Club of Deputies, if an issue would arise, I would say consultation among deputies belonging to the same party, is there anything wrong in that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is perfectly correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, Mr. Stewart, the whole issue is -- I do not know, as a matter of fact, what the issue is. I have -- I'm not a politician, but of course I have observed in my life now and then how parliaments are working. I would be surprised if, within the same party, if an issue arose, if the members of a certain party would not, even intensively, consult each other on what the party line would be if it comes to debate, voting, et cetera. So I'm just wondering what the issue here is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, with respect, I quite agree with Your Honour. Such a party wouldn't be likely to last very long politically, apart from anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So we have to be realistic about it. But, Your Honour, the point, so far as it goes a little bit beyond that, I suggest that what I should do, because I -- it's either -- well, it's either following the implications of what Your Honour has just said. It's either unnecessary for me to ask further questions or it's not realistically practicable for me to ask further questions. But what I suggest that we do at the point this afternoon which Your Honour indicated where we will need to discuss where we're going from here, that discussion will take place in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course it will take place in the absence of the witness. But as I said at the beginning of this hearing, we do that at the very end. But let me just --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'd like to answer that point at the very end, then, Your Honour, is what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, as far as the Chamber is concerned, I consulted with my colleagues that there seems to be nothing unusual in whether or not specifically Mr. Krajisnik or just all of them in the paragraph you've just mentioned, so the Chamber wonders whether there's any need to go further into this matter. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- I think I can say the position is that now that Your Honour says that to me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- then I can say there's no further need. Because Your Honour will understand that with the reassurance that there is nothing lurking then in that paragraph that the Trial Chamber is going to regard as unusual or something to be taken against my client beyond the simple political processes that Your Honour describes, then I don't have a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber deems that there's no need to put any further questions, and this is in relation to the understanding of this paragraph as I just gave to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I ask this, Your Honour: Would the Prosecution be willing for the last two sentences of paragraph 53 to be excised from that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we're not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, to some extent -- Your Honour, may I ask the witness to -- for the witness to leave court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I ask you just to follow Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you continue, Mr. Stewart, I think we should make a clear distinction between what the witness said. He said that he heard from other deputies that ... That's the fact. Second issue is whether that's anything to be considered unusual or uncommon or inappropriate. I do not know, Mr. Hannis, whether you did not accept to excise this part because you wanted to keep the fact as such or whether you wanted to keep any interpretation of those facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we want to keep the fact as such and we want to argue interpretation from it later on at the end of the case in light of all the other evidence. Part of our argument is that Mr. Krajisnik, in addition to whatever authority and power he had as -- in virtue of his position as president of the Assembly and later as member of the expanded presidency he also had de facto power, and we think it goes to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's exactly the point, Your Honour. If it were, and the reason I asked the question was because the first sentence on its own: "In my work in the Assembly I drew the conclusion that Krajisnik was consulted by the deputies of the SDS about all issues." Well, one might squabble a little bit about "all," but really, I wouldn't make a big issue of that. That would reflect the obvious common sense political reality as Your Honour summarised it a few minutes ago. When we go on -- and that sentence on its own would cover the point. The reason why the Prosecution want the other sentences in is, it seems fairly clear, because they -- it's part of their case, and there are a number of other items in this statement that Mr. Krajisnik and the last then in particularly highlights it, that Mr. Krajisnik had more authority and influence with the other members than would be expected from his position because he supplanted the apparently natural person to approach, the chief of the Deputies Club, they tended to go to Mr. Krajisnik instead. So I completely understand that Mr. Hannis -- why Mr. Hannis wishes to preserve it and what he wishes to argue. But it's precisely because he wishes to preserve it and wishes to argue it that I cannot safely leave it like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd be willing to excise the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The last sentence tells us what the witness would consider the appropriate person to address under these circumstances. That's a matter of opinion rather than of fact. Second sentence is about facts, apart from the assessment of whether disputes were likely to arise, which is not a fact but an assessment of a situation. Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's a fact, Your Honour. It's -- with respect, it's a fact. It's that when a witness asserts, and the problem is that the witness makes these assertions in very general terms which then -- and there are a number of these items throughout, in very general terms, which then cannot safely be left. I can't -- the only way I can receive a guarantee, effectively, that these points are safe to leave is if they are taken out. And the Prosecution -- I do understand the Prosecution position. A very generous offer of Mr. Hannis to negotiate by offering me sentence number 3, but I understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The second sentence is bothering you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, yes, Your Honour. It does bother me. And it bothers me, and the reason it bothers me is the other side of the coin from the reason that Mr. Hannis's generous offer is not so generous as to include the second sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The witness may be escorted into the courtroom again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I say, Your Honour, that this welter of memorandums, this is exactly what I have to get hold of and I have to go through with Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I won't say anything more about that right now, Your Honour, in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, I've got a few questions to you. In your statement, in paragraph 53, you say: "Whenever disputes were likely to arise in the parliament, the deputies of the SDS would address Krajisnik for an answer." You've spoken about memorandums, you've spoken about a platform. Could you give any other example of such a situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot this very instant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does this mean that when you talked about memorandum and platform, could you be more precise exactly on what documents you are -- to what documents you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Documents that were items on the agenda and that were debated by the Assembly in the summer of 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How many memorandums are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there was this one document that was authored by the Party of Democratic Action. I'm talking about the session of the summer of 1991. Then there was a document that was authored by the SDP. I think that there was also an SDS proposal at the time, but I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you're talking about two or three memorandums?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The two you specifically mentioned were SDA and SDP documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you be more precise what the subject of these memorandums was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These were offers in terms of how to resolve the Yugoslav crisis. So they reflected the views of the authors of these materials as to how they viewed a solution to the Yugoslav crisis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, specifically, and I start with the SDA memorandum, how did you know that the deputies were addressing Mr. Krajisnik when preparing the position they would take?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is standard organisation for deputies to have their club, and that club has a president. And the president of the club has certain authority, and then all views are double-checked with the president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What you are explaining to me at this moment is that to whom they should have gone. My question was: How exactly did you know that they addressed Mr. Krajisnik in preparing their position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I talked to SDS deputies, or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us names of deputies you were talking to? If you don't know, tell us. Then -- but if you know, please say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have any specific names on my mind now. I gave concrete names in other situations. But I'm talking about this general thing I noticed. When you talk to your colleagues, deputies, you see how a position grows, how it develops. And they, it seems, resolved all their problems with Mr. Krajisnik, not the president of the club.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say "it seems." You talked to your colleagues. You say it seems that they resolved all their problems with Mr. Krajisnik. On the basis of what do you draw the conclusion that -- why did you think that they did so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For example, when you open a new option as a possibility for talks, I know that they go to consult Krajisnik rather than the president of the club.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How do you know that? Did you see them going to the room of Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. They told me that. That is what they would tell me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did they tell you before they did so or did they tell you after they had done so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I was not interested in this post festum. I know, for example that when we worked in our club, and if there was a chance to do something, of course I'd say: I'll look into this with the president of my club. I'd tell them what the exact address is, where I'm going to ask how our views should be formulated. And they would always say that they would see with Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We are at a time where we should have a break anyhow. Of course, the parties can reconsider their position on this issue. Mr. Stewart, the Chamber has understood that you think that you'd need more time for preparation. The Chamber would like you to continue with whatever other issue, again according to the relevance and importance, after the break. We'll adjourn until 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, in paragraph 50 of your statement, and it's a short point, this one, so again, I don't think we need trouble too much with the actual text, but paragraph 50, you talked about the rules of procedure and so on. And then you said, after you talked about Mr. Krajisnik, as you put it, ending the 8th Session, you said: "The SDS members always left the Assembly sessions whenever a possible decision did not suit them." Mr. Bjelobrk, is that not, on reflection, an obvious exaggeration, that they didn't always leave the Assembly sessions whenever a possible decision didn't suit them?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My conclusions were based on the walkout of the SDS MPs and on the summer and the October session of the Assembly, that is, in 1991. And they were in some other cases when the SDS representatives applied such a tactic. That's why I concluded this, that they would leave an Assembly session whenever it suited them. And, as Karadzic said in one of the transcripts we read here, that the decision has to be legitimate to the extent that the representatives of all the national parties have to have their say as to their position with regard to a particular decision to be decided upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bjelobrk. I don't want to subject answers to too much textual analysis, but you said in that answer that they would leave the Assembly session whenever it suited them. Well, Mr. Bjelobrk, I don't wish to cross-examine you about that, because we can probably agree that they would leave when it suited them, and if it didn't suit them, they wouldn't leave, because, well, they were free to come or go. That's a different point from what you say in your statement, which is -- is different. In your statement you're saying not that they left whenever it suited them but that they left -- they always left whenever a possible decision did not suit them. The impression being that just whenever things were not going to their liking, moving in their direction, that they would just get up and leave. Now, I'm putting it to you that it wasn't like that, Mr. Bjelobrk, was it?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine. That's what you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, I don't say anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, let's try to get things straight. How often -- how many times you remember that the SDS members left the Assembly in a situation as you described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I remember that it was that once in the summer session, then there was the October session, where they also walked out, and then there were other situations. But I would have to consult with documents. There must have been -- there definitely were other such situations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Approximately. Was it all together four times, that means the two you mentioned and two others, or was it ten times, or was it 30 times? What is in your recollection, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will tell you that approximately at least five to six times they walked out at the session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then did it ever happen that they did not leave the Assembly, although -- I'm not talking about what kind of issues - although they were outvoted by a majority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But this usually happened when some legislative proposals were tabled that had nothing to do with those other legislative issues I was talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I do understand that what Mr. Stewart described as a rather demonstrative way of expressing their discontent, that that happened a couple of times, whereas usually on less sensitive issues, that they usually would just stay, even if there was a risk of being outvoted. Is that a correct understanding? Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And in the same paragraph, the next sentence, you say: "Likewise, Krajisnik would interrupt the session and break the course of a discussion whenever it did not suit him." Well, first of all, I'll put it in the -- invite you in the general terms. Mr. Bjelobrk, I put it to you: That also is an exaggeration, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, it is no exaggeration.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's be specific. How many times do you say that, when you were present, did Mr. Krajisnik interrupt the session and break the course of a discussion because it did not suit him?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two ways in which a session could be discontinued. One, which is in the paragraph 54, and that's the adjournment of a session. And the other was simply a break in a discussion in order to carry out some consultations [as interpreted] to improve the work of the session and the Assembly. My experience shows that these good intentions always resulted in there not being any agreement, and, based on these statistical figures, I came to a conclusion that the purpose of it all was for the Assembly not to take certain decisions and not to take certain views.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, there was something missing, I'm told, by Ms. Cmeric, from the English transcript, which is demonstrated, I think. Where it says at line 16: "And the other was simply a break in a discussion in order to carry out some consultations," Ms. Cmeric tells me that it missed a phrase, which in English would be, so it would go: "And the other was simply a break in a discussion in order with good intentions to carry out some consultations." And in fact you then referred to these good intentions in the next sentence. So does that make sense to you, Mr. Bjelobrk, the way I've just described your answer? You referred to good intentions twice.

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The break in a session was done with good intentions, in order to improve the organisational aspect of the work of the session. In that sense, these were good intentions. However, if you do your best then not to have the session resume its work, then this becomes an obstruction of the work.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you say, do you, that Mr. Krajisnik then obstructed the work in that way, by preventing the session from resuming its work?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What you describe, Mr. Bjelobrk, would you agree, seems to be this: That if there was a difficult issue where agreement clearly wasn't emerging with the Assembly, then with good intentions, it would be broken off to see whether, behind the scenes, possibly with a smaller group or perhaps more influential group, it could be sorted out, but that, well, in general, it wasn't sorted out? Is that an accurate summary of what happened?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not quite. First of all, a parliament is, by the very definition, a venue where agreements are to be reached, and it was quite natural if the work was to break off, that that particular break would be used for some sort of consultations that would enable the work of the parliament. I've talked about this already. This other part which related to the possibility of finding solutions outside the parliamentary session was already allowing for some parallel lines of work which had nothing to do with the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So when you say Mr. Krajisnik obstructed the work by preventing the session from resuming, can we be clear how that worked mechanically. Are you saying that if, for example, we looked at the minutes, we would find that the session was adjourned by the Speaker, by the president, Mr. Krajisnik; we would see, would we, some reference to it being adjourned for discussions; and then we would find that the session never resumed on that particular date? Is that what we would expect to find in the minutes to represent the sort of obstruction that you've just described?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if we're talking here about one day, one single day, as you've mentioned in your example.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, you described it as being on a number of occasions. So I'm asking you about -- well, any of the days when you say that Mr. Krajisnik obstructed the work by preventing the session from resuming.

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said, in relation to that latter part, that the breaks were very frequent and very long. As a result, we could never reach any conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you say "very long," do you mean hours or are you talking about breaks for days?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most frequently, for a couple of hours. And I want to make myself clear. It is a democratic way of working by placing a proposal on the table and then having the MPs say their opinions on them. However, we never came to that stage where a proposal would be discussed. We had those endless breaks, and simply we were unable to get to the point where a conclusion would be adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you ever present on an occasion when Mr. Krajisnik was asked by anybody from any of the parties to resume the full Assembly session and refused?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the case only at the 8th Session, when he adjourned the session. He was then asked to resume the session, but he didn't want to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, that's -- you're talking about that one on the 14th -- 10th, 11th, 12th, 13th, 14th, 15th October, aren't you, the 8th Session?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But we've had a lot of evidence from you so far on that, but just leave that one aside. Otherwise, were you ever present on any occasion when Mr. Krajisnik was asked by anybody, from any of the parties, to resume the full Assembly session and refused?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the only case of the adjournment of the session as such. I was talking about other types of situations when I was talking about these endless breaks yielding no results whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, would you allow me. If you have covered this subject. Because I would have one additional question. If you didn't reach any agreement during these breaks, would finally the matter be put to a vote or what would then happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the problem, in point. You made a more specific question. It is customary that when you have a point you want to discuss that you put it forth to the MPs to discuss it, or you simply put it to somebody else to decide about what the course of the discussion should be. Whenever anyone would come out with a proposal, we would immediately have consultations follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us an example of an issue which was discussed or where you were about to discuss the issue, then you would have a break, and then, finally, it was -- well, it never ended in any decision? Could you give us an example of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's take the following example. At both of these sessions, there was the proposal for the -- for Bosnia and Herzegovina to take a certain view with regard to the Yugoslav crisis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me stop you here. It is -- we heard a lot of evidence on the, well, let's say the very problematic issue of the future of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that every party, the parties took a quite different position, that they could not reach an agreement, that -- well, what happened there. Apart from that, any other issue. So not the future of a state or a republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, whether or not independent; another issue, where, through breaks, finally never a conclusion was adopted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot mention any other points, because they were simply of less significance and did not elicit such a difference in opinion, when I was talking about the memorandums, for example. When you look at the summer sessions, you will see that the Assembly has never decided upon anything like, for instance, the October sessions. If at least we voted on being unanimous in not agreeing upon anything, that would have been something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From listening to your testimony, it appears to be, but please correct me when I'm wrong, that your observations and your statement about the dysfunctioning of the parliament, of the Assembly, which is described in a rather general way, actually happened in relation to that one big issue, that is, what will be the future of Bosnia and Herzegovina, when you're talking about obstruction, when you're talking about these kind of matters, that it was always that one and big subject. Is that a correct understanding? You're nodding, but the transcript doesn't read any nodding.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I do confirm that this is the way it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In your statement, at paragraph 20, you said: "In mid-1991, there were many speeches of the deputies in parliament, stating that Serbs from the various regions 'had to protect themselves.' You could see that the idea came from the top leadership of the SDS." I take it in your statement the phrase "had to protect themselves" is in quotes. I take it that what you were meaning to say then was that that -- that was what those many speeches said or that was some such phrase that they used. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the phrase they used, but that was also the quintessence of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- and when you -- the idea that you say came from the top leadership of the SDS, this is the idea of protecting themselves. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't referring to the leadership having to protect themselves, if I've understood you correctly, but rather to protect the areas where Serbs were a majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No. I didn't express myself sufficiently clearly, then, Mr. Bjelobrk, because that isn't what I meant. The -- you say you could see that the idea came from the top leadership of the SDS. I was just asking you to confirm that the idea that you say had come from the top leadership of the SDS was the idea of the Serbs from the various regions having to protect themselves.

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. So my thesis is that the leadership of the SDS were the authors is based on the understanding of the facts, that in the summer of 1991, there were no meaningful incidents among the population. There was no need to organise any kind of protection or to assume that there should be protection for someone who was a minority amongst you. So, since these were the first regions that were supposed to be organised, namely, Romanija, eastern Herzegovina, Bosanska Krajina, as areas with a majority Serb population, there were no local reasons to have this done, so the only thing that remained was the concept that the leadership of the party had.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So this is a -- can I get it straight: This is a thesis of yours - you may not be the only person to have held this thesis, but this is what you describe as your thesis, is actually based on reasoning and inference; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was involved in this kind of public work. I held office and I had to think about these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So when you say you could see that the idea came from the top leadership of the SDS, you don't have any direct knowledge of instructions to that effect?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a simple reason: Because in politics, not everything is televised [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I think your answer there started although it hasn't appeared in the English transcript. I think your answer started with no and then, "For a simple reason." I'm not sure who is going to confirm that for me, but ... You said when I said you didn't have any direct knowledge, you were basically agreeing and then giving the reason why you didn't? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have understood me properly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In paragraph 59 of your statement, you referred to -- you say: "I recall that Nikola Koljevic published a text about human resettlement in 1991, which was part of the wider discussion on resettlement which I mentioned before." There's no other title or name given. Are you able to help with anything more specific by way of identification of Mr. Koljevic's text?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The elements that I have for identification, in terms of my own memory, is that this was published by the Sarajevo newspaper Oslobodjenje, and I think that the text was published somewhere on the second page, towards the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, that's quite specific as far as pages are concerned, Mr. Bjelobrk.

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you asked me about identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm expressing appreciation, Mr. Bjelobrk, for it being very specific. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's as far as I'm able to go this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would first have at this moment one additional question to you, Mr. Bjelobrk, and that is: You explained to us that you could see that the speeches claiming that the Serbs had to protect themselves came from the SDS leadership. Now, you explained that you saw no need, looking at the situation on the ground, you saw no need for any protection. You also told us that in the Assembly, SDS deputies were making speeches, indicating that there was need to protect themselves. These are two facts. Now, what made you believe that this idea came from the SDS leadership rather than from foreign politicians, the president of what was left from Yugoslavia, well, from whomever? What made you believe that it came from the SDS leadership?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I tried to convey what I know about this and what my experience was, I primarily focused on what I believe was done in Bosnia-Herzegovina itself. Otherwise, I think that the entire concept, in terms of everything that was going on in Bosnia-Herzegovina in respect to the problem that we are discussing, is based on a major influence played by Serbia and Croatia respectively. So there was a major foreign influence involved. However --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you again. I asked for specific facts, although I might not have been clear enough, specific facts on why you think that this idea came from the SDS leadership.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The very fact that these regional communities were constituted meant that it was the top echelons of the SDS that had authored it. That is what was made public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Made public when and by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the moment when it would be made public. I already mentioned something like that. The public would find out only when it would be told that: Yesterday a session had been held of the Assembly of that particular region. And that is how you realise that this kind of regional community had been established in the first place. In the previous analyses, people who were close, like MPs or other politicians, they would pick up bits and pieces and realise that something like that would eventually happen. And, of course, they had much more information, therefore, than the general public did. And, thirdly, if you tried to understand the people who live in a particular area, you're probably going to do that through elementary statistics, in terms of what is actually happening to those people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do I understand you well that, first of all, we're talking -- we were talking about speeches made concerning the need for protection, protection of Serbs. You said these speeches were -- the idea for that protection came from the SDS leadership. Now, when you explained that to us, I understood your answer to be that, on the basis of the pattern you saw, where it happened, that it at a certain moment became public, so on the basis of that pattern, that your conclusion was that the idea must have come from the SDS leadership.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there anything else, apart from the pattern you saw, that any specific fact that would support that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far back as August or September 1991, I heard partial discussions of persons from the SDS who then said that the Serbs should have their own government, the Croats should have their own government, and the Bosniaks should have their own government. And I inferred on that basis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is, you heard people talking about separation of ethnicities. But the subject of our discussion was that the need to protect yourself was an idea that came from the SDS leadership. That's, of course, something different from separating several ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An idea always comes from a small group of people. It may, over a given period of time, be espoused by a large number of people. But even if you look at a hypothesis and if you wonder how many people can stand behind an idea, it will probably be based on something that came as a challenge, at least at first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I, as a citizen, would want protection, even without any kind of political representation, the very first second I'd feel threatened. However, when there is no justification for feeling threatened, then the theory of protection can only be engendered among a small group of people who put this in the context of a political vision and then work from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you told us already that you couldn't imagine anyone else than the SDS leadership to be that small group of people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, you told us that you had no specific facts, apart from the pattern, apart from the widespread -- the idea being widespread, apart from that, you had no specific reason to assume that it was the SDS leadership rather than any other small group you might have had in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is my own logical thinking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Hannis, is there any need to put further questions to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Not at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi has one or more questions to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Normally speaking, the Bench of course will ask questions from time to time, but the -- what we seem to be engaged in now is what conventionally happens when cross-examination has finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Which, Your Honour, is not, as I understand it, the position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I should have been more clear, Mr. Stewart. The question Judge El Mahdi is going to put to the witness was a question the Chamber had in mind to put to this witness already prior to this moment and which I have forgotten to ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's no problem at all about that. I just wanted to verify because, of course, it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether the cross-examination has been finished or not is a matter still to be decided.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I remember what Your Honour said earlier. No, Your Honour, of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we have one question now and you'll be given an opportunity to -- Judge El Mahdi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] Witness, I would like to remind you of the question that was put to you concerning paragraph 53 of your statement. I think you have the declaration before you, in front of you: Paragraph 53 reads as follows, and I shall be quoting this, reading this in English: [In English] "...were likely to arise." Disputes -- I beg your pardon. "Whenever disputes were likely to arise in the parliament, the deputies of the SDS would address Krajisnik for an answer, even though the chief of the club was the person to whom they should turn to." [Interpretation] My question is a very simple one: Can you tell us or give us names of some of those MPs who expressed their concern because they had to turn to Mr. Krajisnik? Does anything come to mind? Could you give us some names, or just a few names of some of these MPs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could not remember exactly now. I couldn't remember the names. I tried to present my own way of understanding this here. When there were different views and when I tried to talk to colleagues from the SDS, at the same time, I would check who the authorities they consulted were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were these -- are you talking about one MP or two MPs, no more than that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was certainly at the level of, say, 10 or 15 MPs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Over a period of a few months?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A year, if you multiply this by 15, one MP may have told you the same thing two or three times, in other words, that he needs to look into the matter more closely with the president of the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. In those 15 or so times -- or actually, this Assembly was constituted sometime in the autumn of 1990, and we had a joint experience of one year. There was a political necessity for you to see with your colleagues who their persons in authority were. And whenever you discuss any issue, you would come to realise who these persons were. Sometimes it would be better; sometimes it would be worse. Any time I talked to other MPs, including MPs from the SDS, I tried to see who these people were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I'm sure that you discussed this with members of other parties. I'm sure you discussed this with members of the SDA. So they were referring to -- or they turned to the president of their club or the president of their party. Whom did they refer to? Whom did they turn to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here I talked about relations within the Assembly, not outside the Assembly. I'll be very precise. I will say that outside the Assembly, Radovan Karadzic was the highest authority in the SDS, like Alija Izetbegovic was in the SDA, or the president of the HDZ, for persons from the HDZ. Within the Assembly, though, you would have the nominal position of the head of a club, but that would not mean that he was the greatest parliamentary authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand. But at the Assembly itself, I think -- but correct me if I'm wrong, please -- I think that the president of the club is not an important person in the Assembly itself; it's outside the Assembly that he plays a major role. They prepare their work and they exchange their views at their club. I think in the Assembly itself, you could address the president of the Assembly if you wanted to, or were you not allowed to do this? In other words, this was not prohibited; you were perfectly entitled to address the president of the Assembly, I believe.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course it was not prohibited. Anybody could address the president of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So did you address the president of the Assembly yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. I'd ask him to take the floor or to start an initiative as an MP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... outside the Assembly sessions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One can talk to the president of the Assembly and couloirs and during committee meetings and the like, and then we are all in the capacity of members of these committees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand. But basically you talked about meetings with 10 or 15 MPs or so. That is what you based your opinion on and that's how you outlined a general trend, on the basis of this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be very precise, the impression I got was that the top authority among the MPs in parliament was Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is your personal feeling about it. [In English] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stewart, the Chamber has allowed, exceptionally, Mr. Krajisnik to put questions to the witness as well if you would consider this wise to do. We didn't hear from him. Do I take it that he has no questions or should I interpret it otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Apart from the fact there's not really time to do it anyway today, but that's a different matter. No. What happened, Your Honour, was that Mr. Krajisnik and I did have -- well, took most of the first break with Ms. Cmeric to talk about this, and what we concluded -- and, Your Honour, behind what we concluded, I do wish to make plain that Mr. Krajisnik and I are not totally agreed on this issue, not surprisingly, because Your Honour remembers that we had a considerable debate on an application by Mr. Krajisnik with a rather ludicrous position of my own client making an application which I then effectively opposed and we argued it out between ourselves and I was largely successful on that application. So there's something remaining of that. But nevertheless, there was a considerable measure of agreement between Mr. Krajisnik and myself this afternoon. But what we did agree about, Your Honour, was that Mr. Krajisnik -- that neither of us wished for Mr. Krajisnik to ask questions today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. That's clear. Then, Mr. Bjelobrk, I'd like to ask you to follow the usher and leave the courtroom for a while, but at the same time, I'd like you to remain standby at least for the next ten minutes, because we have to deal with a procedural issue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, as indicated before, the Chamber would like to give you an opportunity to tell us what you'd still have to deal with during any further cross-examination you would like to conduct. If you would consider this better, because it of course reveals some of the, well, Defence strategy, perhaps, which you would rather not make public because this is a matter of procedural order rather than anything else, you, of course, could apply to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, with respect, I do. That does seem a fair suggestion, and I would like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- take advantage of it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now we are, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I haven't counted up, but I've identified something like 12 to 15, something like 12 to 15 significant points, some of which the Prosecution have responded to Your Honour's suggestion by indicating they would drop them from the evidence altogether, some of which they have resisted or -- don't criticise them for that, Your Honour, they're on the other side of the case, but they have resisted or expressed their agreement in qualified, sometimes heavy qualified terms, some of the points the Prosecution have, well, frankly refusing to excise, which is their prerogative to say that that's their position. So we are left -- well, two things -- three things, really. We are left, first of all, with a significant residue of important points. Secondly, Your Honour, I really produce these indications in summary to indicate why it's necessary to have this witness back for cross-examination. But, Your Honour, I've also indicated the other matters which Mr. Krajisnik wished to explore. And, Your Honour, the fact is, we did not have an enormous amount of time with this witness, given the huge range of topics that he covers. And for his -- for these matters now, in this incomplete way, to be reduced, doesn't mean that I haven't been faced with this entire statement, which I have, right up until now, as what I had to prepare for for cross-examination. And recently, alongside the transcripts of his evidence. And I made it very clear yesterday afternoon, Your Honour, that I couldn't realistically attempt to prepare for and cover the entire ground of his cross-examination for today, and I do submit that it's absolutely plain in the light of the run-through that I have just offered to the Trial Chamber in addition to -- I do believe I can fairly claim the fairly extensive ground that we have covered at a perfectly reasonable pace today in cross-examination, it is quite clear that this cross-examination is just not finished. And, Your Honour, we are balancing something which is -- none of us wants to bring witnesses backwards and forwards unnecessarily, but in the end, all we're asking for is that a witness returns to have his cross-examination completed, and that is what it is. And I appreciate the Trial Chamber wants to go to helpful lengths to see if we can avoid witnesses coming back a second time unnecessarily, but we do seem to be -- everybody bending over backwards and pushing it to the limits, really simply without being dismissive of Mr. Bjelobrk, simply to avoid a witness having to come back on another day to have his cross-examination completed, when it really is apparent -- if it were tomorrow and we could sit tomorrow, Mr. Bjelobrk were here, we'd suggest nobody would seriously be saying that the cross-examination should finish tonight and he shouldn't come back tomorrow and it shouldn't continue, and to apply some different test and different approach altogether because he is going to have to go back and he is going to suffer the inconvenience, which we acknowledge, of coming back, is not the right approach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. Mr. Hannis, any --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No comment on that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At this moment, the Chamber will not give a final decision on whether or not this cross-examination is finished. First of all, the parties are invited to see to what extent they can agree on the issues you, Mr. Stewart, has mentioned as matters that would still need further cross-examination. That's one. Second, the Chamber wants to consider, also on the basis of the outcome of any conversations between the parties, whether the remaining portions of the evidence in writing are fit to be admitted at all. I mean, we're talking about a statement of a witness which is a witness of fact. So, therefore, it could well be that if the Chamber considers this not to be facts but, rather, opinion, et cetera, that the Chamber might not fully admit the statement of the witness into evidence. Then at that very moment, when we have heard what the parties tell us, when the Chamber has considered whether the statement could be admitted into evidence, yes or no, then, of course, we'll see what the points are that are remaining. Then the Chamber will also -- because this Chamber is not guided by financial aspects and whether it bothers a witness or not, but certainly bears, as everyone in this house, I would say, some responsibility for how the funds are spent in this Tribunal, especially knowing that funding of this Tribunal is not without any problem, we have to find an efficient solution. So we still then could consider, whether if we would consider it a right decision to say that cross-examination has not yet finished, whether a videolink would be a way out for these other reasons or not. So we'll not give a decision at this moment, finally, on whether the Chamber considers that the Defence has had sufficient opportunity to cross-examine this witness. Mr. Krajisnik, I saw that you would like to address the Chamber. We have to be careful, because we might run out of tape very quickly. So if you would limit it to just the essence of what you'd like to say. Mr. Krajisnik, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I wish to thank you for giving me the opportunity to address the witness and put certain documents to him. I agreed with my lawyer, because I thought that this examination would be deferred, so I thought that it would happen during our next session. If, by any chance, you do not bring this witness back, could we please use these arguments nevertheless? Because you will clarify some matters. This is a very important witness. He's not a Serb, or rather, he is not from the SDS, but he will throw light on what happened in parliament. I assure you, Your Honours, that you will find out that what he said was wrong. He thinks that I'm against them, but I did vote for their proposal, so he will realise that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, that's exactly the reason why the Chamber invited the Defence to come up with the literal text of stenographic notes of those meetings. We could then look at them, as I said, and we could then decide whether it would be -- whether it would be appropriate to recall the witness in order to confront him with that or that we would do without. That's a decision still to be taken on the basis of any material we might receive. Then I'd like to ask Mr. Usher to escort the witness into the courtroom again. I'll do it really quickly. Tapes are -- it's over. Yes. I know how important it is to have everything on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I nevertheless will address Mr. Bjelobrk, and everything I'll say to him will be confirmed in writing, a copy to be sent to the parties. Mr. Bjelobrk, the Defence would like to put more questions to you in cross-examination. The Chamber has not yet decided whether you would be recalled to appear again in order to be further examined. The Chamber will still have to decide that. You'll be informed about the decision of this Chamber. You'll not stay in The Hague for the time being, because the Chamber will not be sitting during the next week, not tomorrow, which is a holiday, not next week. This will be confirmed to you in writing. You are instructed, in this uncertain situation, not to speak with anyone about the testimony you have given or, eventually, are still about to give. This instruction is valid, first of all, until you receive information. If that information will be that you'll not be recalled, then it's not valid anymore, although I don't know whether it's wise to discuss with everyone your testimony in this court. But it's public testimony. If the information will be that you will be recalled, then the instruction continues to be applicable. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is clear. I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may follow the usher, who will escort you out of the courtroom. And I think you already, in case you would not return, I thank you for having come to The Hague and to have answered all the questions in this courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as the parties are concerned, to be quite honest, I do not know what the procedure is, if we're running out of a tape, it never happened to me in the last couple of years.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I suggest we have a transcript at our next session, I think perhaps when we're on the record, on tape, we can describe what we've done since the tape ran out tonight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I'm seeking to do is to at least make clear on the record that we ran out of tape, there's no audio record, and therefore, I kept it rather brief at this very moment. Then I take it -- I beg the parties not to raise any further procedural issues unless really necessary, because we have no audiotape. I don't know whether we still have a videotape, but that usually also records the -- Madam Registrar says no. Is there any urgent issue to be raised at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm tempted just to shake my head, Your Honour, because it wouldn't make much difference. But no, there isn't, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll adjourn. We'll not sit tomorrow, which is a UN holiday, we'll not sit next week, and we'll resume on the 22nd of November, I think at 9.00 in the morning, as far as I remember. I do not know which courtroom exactly, but, Madam Registrar ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we sit on the 22nd November at 9.00, in Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn until the 22nd of November, 9.00, Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 22nd day of November, 2004, at 9.00 a.m. 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.32 p.m.,
